passages.p1: Six friends A, B, C, D, E and F sit in a straight row, all facing north. The positions are numbered 1 to 6 from the left end. B sits at one of the extreme ends. A sits second to the right of B. D sits at the other extreme end. C sits immediately to the right of A. F sits adjacent to D.
passages.p2:
Five colleagues P, Q, R, S and T live on five different floors of a building, numbered 1 (lowest) to 5 (topmost), one person per floor. Each of them drinks a different beverage in the morning: tea, coffee, juice, milk or water.
Q lives on the floor immediately above R. T lives above S but not on the topmost floor. P lives above R. S lives above Q. The person on floor 3 drinks tea. The person on the topmost floor drinks coffee. R drinks milk. Q does not drink juice.

questions.text:
Select the option that is related to the third number in the same way as the second number is related to the first.

27 : 3 :: 64 : ?
questions.explanation: 27 is 3³, so the second number is the cube root of the first. The cube root of 64 is 4.
steps: 27 = 3 × 3 × 3, so 3 is the cube root of 27
Apply the same relation: cube root of 64
4 × 4 × 4 = 64, so the answer is 4
questions.trap: Taking the square root because 64 is a perfect square.
questions.revise: Squares, cubes and their roots up to 20
wrongReasons: Divided 64 by 4 without finding the relation
Took the square root of 64
Halved 64 without finding the relation
questions.shortcut: Check small perfect cubes first: 27 and 64 are both cubes (3³, 4³).

questions.text:
Select the option that is related to the third letter-cluster in the same way as the second is related to the first.

ACE : GIK :: BDF : ?
questions.explanation: Each letter of ACE moves 6 places forward to give GIK (A→G, C→I, E→K). Apply +6 to B, D, F: B→H, D→J, F→L.
steps: A→G, C→I, E→K: every letter moves +6
B+6 = H
D+6 = J
F+6 = L, so the cluster is HJL
questions.trap: Shifting only the first letter, or using +7 after a slip in counting.
wrongReasons: Repeated the second cluster unchanged
Shifted only the first letter by 6
Shifted every letter by 7 instead of 6
questions.shortcut: Compare only the first letters (A→G = +6); the others follow the same step.

questions.text: Choose the option that relates to 'Pascal' in the same way as 'Ampere' relates to 'Current'.
questions.explanation: Ampere is the SI unit of electric current. Pascal is the SI unit of pressure.
steps: Ampere measures current
Pascal measures pressure (force per unit area)
Force, energy and power have the units newton, joule and watt
questions.trap: Choosing force because pressure is derived from it.
questions.revise: SI units and the quantities they measure
wrongReasons: Newton, not pascal, is the unit of force
Joule, not pascal, is the unit of energy
Watt, not pascal, is the unit of power
questions.approach: Match the unit to the quantity it measures directly, not to a related quantity.

questions.text: Select the odd one out.
questions.explanation: 144 = 12², 196 = 14² and 225 = 15² are perfect squares. 250 is not a perfect square (15² = 225, 16² = 256).
steps: Check each number against nearby squares
250 lies between 225 and 256, so it is not a square
questions.trap: Looking for a pattern in the differences instead of testing squares.
wrongReasons: Perfect square (12²)
Perfect square (14²)
Perfect square (15²)
questions.shortcut: Squares up to 20² should be known by heart; spot the non-square instantly.

steps: Spot what the question tests: Water image = top-bottom swap.
Option A (Figure A) is out: This is the left-right mirror image.
Option B (Figure B) is out: This is a rotation.
Option C (Figure C) is out: This is both flips, i.e. a 180° rotation.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing the left-right inversion.
So the answer is option D: Figure D.
questions.trap: Choosing the left-right inversion.
wrongReasons: This is the left-right mirror image
This is a rotation
This is both flips, i.e. a 180° rotation

questions.text:
What should come in place of the question mark in the series?

5, 6, 14, 45, 184, ?
questions.trap: Seeing only a growing multiplier and forgetting the matching addition.
questions.revise: Series with changing multiplier and addend
wrongReasons: Added 10 instead of 5 after multiplying
Multiplied 184 by 5 but forgot the + 5
Repeated the last multiplier (×4) instead of moving to ×5
questions.shortcut: If the growth is faster than doubling, test 'n × k + k' with k = 1, 2, 3…

questions.text:
What should come in place of the question mark in the series?

4, 6, 12, 30, 90, ?
questions.explanation: The multipliers are 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3 and then 3.5: 4 → 6 → 12 → 30 → 90 → 315.
steps: The next multiplier is 3.5: 90 × 3.5 = 315
questions.trap: Stopping at multiplier 3 and picking 270 as the continuation.
wrongReasons: Multiplied 90 by 3 instead of 3.5
Multiplied 90 by 4
Added 210 without a rule
questions.shortcut: Write the ratios between consecutive terms first; here they climb by 0.5.

questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 210 110" role="img"><rect x="5" y="5" width="100" height="100" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><text x="12" y="120" font-size="0"></text><g transform="translate(5,5)"><rect x="0" y="0" width="50" height="50" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="30" cy="20" r="6" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/></g><path d="M5 5 L105 5 L105 105 L5 105 Z" stroke="#999" stroke-dasharray="4" fill="none" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="55" y1="5" x2="55" y2="105" stroke="#999" stroke-dasharray="4"/><line x1="5" y1="55" x2="105" y2="55" stroke="#999" stroke-dasharray="4"/><text x="115" y="30" font-size="11">Folded twice,</text><text x="115" y="45" font-size="11">hole punched in</text><text x="115" y="60" font-size="11">the top-left</text><text x="115" y="75" font-size="11">quarter</text></svg>
questions.explanation: Each fold reflects the hole across the fold line, so one punch gives four holes, one in each quarter, placed symmetrically about both centre lines.
steps: Spot what the question tests: Fold line = mirror line for punched holes.
Option A (Figure A) is out: Only two holes: it misses the second fold.
Option B (Figure B) is out: Only two holes on a diagonal, which ignores one fold.
Option C (Figure C) is out: Has a stray hole at the centre and a missing quarter.
Common slip to avoid: Forgetting that two folds give four holes, or placing the extra holes diagonally only.
So the answer is option D: Figure D.
questions.trap: Forgetting that two folds give four holes, or placing the extra holes diagonally only.
questions.revise: Fold line = mirror line for punched holes

Only two holes on a diagonal, which ignores one fold
Has a stray hole at the centre and a missing quarter

questions.text: In a certain code language, MARKET is written as NCUOJZ. How will BASKET be written in that code?
questions.explanation: In MARKET → NCUOJZ the letters move +1, +2, +3, +4, +5, +6 in order. Apply the same to BASKET: B+1=C, A+2=C, S+3=V, K+4=O, E+5=J, T+6=Z.
steps: Apply to BASKET: B+1 = C
Code: CCVOJZ
questions.trap: Applying a constant shift of +1 to every letter.
wrongReasons: Shifted the second letter by 1 instead of 2
Shifted K by 5 instead of 4
Shifted B by 2 instead of 1
questions.shortcut: Only the first three letters differ from MARKET (B, A, S); the last three (K, E, T) are unchanged, so the answer ends in OJZ.

questions.text: In a certain code language, 'sun moon star' is written as 'ka ni po', 'moon rain cloud' is written as 'po ta ze' and 'star tree' is written as 'ni ma'. What is the code for 'sun'?
questions.explanation: 'moon' is common to the first two statements and 'po' is common to their codes, so moon = po. 'star' is common to the first and third statements and 'ni' is common to their codes, so star = ni. The remaining code in the first statement, 'ka', is for 'sun'.
steps: Statements 1 and 2 share 'moon' and the code 'po', so moon = po
Statements 1 and 3 share 'star' and the code 'ni', so star = ni
Statement 1 has codes ka, ni, po for sun, star, moon
Remove ni and po: sun = ka
questions.trap: Matching codes by position instead of by the common word.
wrongReasons: That is the code for 'star'
That is the code for 'moon'
That is the code for 'rain' or 'cloud'
questions.approach: Find the word common to two statements, then the code common to the same two statements.

questions.text: In a certain code, every letter is replaced by the letter at the same position from the opposite end of the alphabet (A↔Z, B↔Y, and so on). How will PLANE be written in that code?
questions.explanation: The letter at position n is replaced by the letter at position 27 − n. P (16) → 11 = K, L (12) → 15 = O, A (1) → 26 = Z, N (14) → 13 = M, E (5) → 22 = V.
steps: Use position sum 27: P(16) → 11 = K
E(5) → 22 = V; code is KOZMV
questions.trap: Using 26 instead of 27 and landing one letter off.
wrongReasons: Replaced N by N instead of M
Replaced L by P instead of O
Replaced P by J instead of K
questions.shortcut: Letter pairs add up to 27: A–Z, B–Y, … M–N; remember them as mirror images.

questions.text: Select the Venn diagram that best represents the relationship among: Women (W), Mothers (M), Doctors (D).
optionFigures: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 120 100" role="img"><circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><text x="46" y="21" font-size="10">W</text><circle cx="105" cy="30" r="12" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><text x="101" y="34" font-size="10">M</text><circle cx="88" cy="74" r="20" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><text x="84" y="78" font-size="10">D</text></svg>

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 120 100" role="img"><circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><text x="46" y="21" font-size="10">W</text><circle cx="36" cy="56" r="16" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><text x="32" y="60" font-size="10">M</text><circle cx="72" cy="56" r="22" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><text x="68" y="60" font-size="10">D</text></svg>

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 120 100" role="img"><circle cx="30" cy="50" r="22" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><text x="26" y="54" font-size="10">W</text><circle cx="60" cy="50" r="22" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><text x="56" y="54" font-size="10">M</text><circle cx="90" cy="50" r="22" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><text x="86" y="54" font-size="10">D</text></svg>
questions.explanation: All mothers are women, so M lies inside W. Some doctors are women and some may be mothers, so D overlaps both W and M.
steps: Spot what the question tests: Venn: subset, overlap, disjoint.
Option A (Figure A) is out: Mothers sit outside women, which is false.
Option C (Figure C) is out: Mothers and doctors are swapped.
Option D (Figure D) is out: Women, mothers and doctors are drawn as separate sets.
Common slip to avoid: Drawing doctors as separate from mothers.
So the answer is option B: Figure B.
questions.trap: Drawing doctors as separate from mothers.
wrongReasons: Mothers sit outside women, which is false
Mothers and doctors are swapped
Women, mothers and doctors are drawn as separate sets

questions.text:
In a certain code, 'A + B' means 'A is the father of B', 'A − B' means 'A is the sister of B' and 'A × B' means 'A is the mother of B'.

If P × Q − R + S, how is P related to S?
questions.explanation: P × Q: P is the mother of Q. Q − R: Q is the sister of R, so P is also R's mother. R + S: R is the father of S. P is the mother of S's father, so P is S's (paternal) grandmother.
steps: P × Q: P is Q's mother
Q − R: Q and R are siblings, so P is R's mother too
R + S: R is S's father
P is the mother of S's father, so P is S's grandmother
questions.trap: Treating Q as the link to S and calling P an aunt or mother.
wrongReasons: P is two generations above S
P is a generation above R, not directly above S
P is the parent, not the sibling, of R
questions.approach: Write each symbol as a relation in words, then chain them left to right, tracking generations.

questions.text: Ravi starts from his house and walks 17 m towards the north. He then turns right and walks 24 m. Then he turns right again and walks 10 m. How far and in which direction is he now from his house?
questions.explanation: Taking east as +x and north as +y: after 17 m north he is at (0, 17); 24 m east puts him at (24, 17); 10 m south puts him at (24, 7). Distance = √(24² + 7²) = 25 m and he is to the north-east of the house.
steps: North 17 m: (0, 17)
Right turn = east, 24 m: (24, 17)
Right turn = south, 10 m: (24, 7)
Distance = √(24² + 7²) = √625 = 25 m
x and y are both positive, so the direction is North-East
questions.trap: Adding 17 + 10 instead of netting the north-south legs.
wrongReasons: Added the north and south legs instead of subtracting
Ignored the 7 m northward displacement
Used only the first leg for the distance
questions.shortcut: Net displacement is 24 east and 7 north: 7-24-25 is a Pythagorean triple.

questions.text: One morning, soon after sunrise, Ravi and Karan were standing face to face at a crossing. Karan's shadow fell exactly to the left of Ravi. Which direction was Karan facing?
questions.explanation: Morning shadows fall towards the west. The shadow is to Ravi's left, so Ravi's left is west, which means Ravi faces north. Karan faces Ravi, so Karan faces south.
steps: After sunrise the sun is in the east, so shadows fall to the west
The shadow lies on Ravi's left, so Ravi's left = west
If left is west, Ravi faces north
Karan stands face to face with Ravi, so he faces south
questions.trap: Forgetting that morning shadows fall west and taking the left as east.
questions.revise: Shadow problems: morning shadow west, evening shadow east
wrongReasons: That is the direction Ravi faces
The shadow would then fall behind Karan
The shadow would then fall in front of Karan
questions.shortcut: Morning: the shadow points west. Whoever has the shadow on the left is facing north.

questions.text: In a row of students, Anil is 14th from the left end and Binod is 19th from the right end. If they interchange their positions, Anil becomes 26th from the left end. How many students are there in the row?
questions.explanation: After the interchange, Anil occupies Binod's original place, which is 26th from the left. Binod's original place is also 19th from the right. Total = 26 + 19 − 1 = 44.
steps: Anil's new place = Binod's old place = 26th from left
Binod's old place is also 19th from right
questions.trap: Using Anil's old position (14) in the formula.
questions.revise: Total in a row: left rank + right rank − 1
wrongReasons: Added 26 and 19 without subtracting 1
Used the original positions 14 and 26
Subtracted 1 twice instead of once
questions.shortcut: One person's left rank and right rank always add up to total + 1.

questions.text: A 4 x 4 grid is shown. How many squares of all sizes are there in the figure?
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 180 180" role="img"><rect x="10" y="10" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="50" y="10" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="90" y="10" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="130" y="10" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="10" y="50" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="50" y="50" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="90" y="50" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="130" y="50" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="10" y="90" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="50" y="90" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="90" y="90" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="130" y="90" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="10" y="130" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="50" y="130" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="90" y="130" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="130" y="130" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/></svg>
steps: Spot what the question tests: Squares in an n x n grid = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6.
Option A (16) is out: Only 1x1 squares counted.
Option B (29) is out: One square missed, probably the 4x4.
Option D (36) is out: Squares of one size counted twice.
Common slip to avoid: Counting only the 16 small squares.
So the answer is option C: 30.
questions.trap: Counting only the 16 small squares.
questions.revise: Squares in an n x n grid = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6
wrongReasons: Only 1x1 squares counted
One square missed, probably the 4x4
Squares of one size counted twice

questions.text:
Statements:
All pens are books.
Some books are tables.
No table is a chair.

Conclusions:
I. Some pens are tables.
II. Some books are not chairs.
III. No pen is a chair.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
options: All I, II and III follow
questions.explanation: Some books are tables and no table is a chair, so those books are not chairs: II follows. Nothing links pens to tables (I) or to chairs (III) definitely.
steps: Draw 'pens' inside 'books'; 'tables' overlaps part of 'books'
The books that are tables are not chairs, so some books are not chairs: II follows
The pens may or may not touch the table part: I does not follow
Pens may or may not be chairs outside the table part: III does not follow
questions.trap: Treating a possible overlap as a certain one.
wrongReasons: I is only a possibility: pens may or may not be among the table-books
I and III are possibilities, not certainties
III is not forced: pens could still be chairs through some other route
questions.approach: Draw the minimal diagram; accept a conclusion only if it holds in every valid drawing.

questions.text: A grid of 3 rows and 4 columns is shown. How many squares of all sizes does it contain?
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 180 140" role="img"><rect x="10" y="10" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="50" y="10" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="90" y="10" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="130" y="10" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="10" y="50" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="50" y="50" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="90" y="50" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="130" y="50" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="10" y="90" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="50" y="90" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="90" y="90" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="130" y="90" width="40" height="40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/></svg>
steps: Spot what the question tests: Squares in an m x n grid = sum of (m-k+1)(n-k+1).
Option A (12) is out: Only 1x1 squares counted.
Option C (18) is out: 3x3 squares forgotten.
Option D (24) is out: Rectangles counted along with squares.
Common slip to avoid: Counting only the 12 small squares or forgetting the 3x3 squares.
So the answer is option B: 20.
questions.trap: Counting only the 12 small squares or forgetting the 3x3 squares.
questions.revise: Squares in an m x n grid = sum of (m-k+1)(n-k+1)
wrongReasons: Only 1x1 squares counted
3x3 squares forgotten
Rectangles counted along with squares

questions.text: Who sits third from the right end of the row?
questions.explanation: B is at the left end (position 1) because A is second to its right and B is at an extreme. A is at 3, C at 4 (immediately right of A), D at 6 (other extreme), F at 5 (adjacent to D) and E at 2. Third from the right is position 4: C.
steps: B must be at the left end, since A sits two places to its right
D takes the right end: 6
F is adjacent to D: 5, so E = 2
Order: B, E, A, C, F, D; third from the right = C
questions.trap: Counting positions from the wrong end.
wrongReasons: E sits second from the left
A is third from the left
F sits second from the right

questions.text: How many triangles are there in the following figure?
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 240 150" role="img"><polygon points="120.0,10 10,140 230,140" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><line x1="120.0" y1="10" x2="54.0" y2="140" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><line x1="120.0" y1="10" x2="98.0" y2="140" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><line x1="120.0" y1="10" x2="142.0" y2="140" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><line x1="120.0" y1="10" x2="186.0" y2="140" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/></svg>
questions.explanation: Six lines meet at the apex, so any two of them with the base form a triangle: C(6,2) = 15.
steps: Spot what the question tests: Triangles = C(k,2) for k lines from the apex.
Option B (5) is out: Only the smallest triangles counted.
Option C (10) is out: Triangles using the sloping sides are missed.
Option D (21) is out: One extra line assumed.
Common slip to avoid: Counting only the 5 small triangles.
So the answer is option A: 15.
questions.trap: Counting only the 5 small triangles.
questions.revise: Triangles = C(k,2) for k lines from the apex
wrongReasons: Only the smallest triangles counted
Triangles using the sloping sides are missed
One extra line assumed

questions.text: Which beverage does Q drink?
questions.explanation: Q is just above R and S is above Q; T is above S but not on top. Only R1, Q2, S3, T4, P5 fits, so S (floor 3) drinks tea.
steps: Q = R + 1 and S > Q; T > S with T not on floor 5, and P > R
Only R1, Q2, S3, T4, P5 satisfies all of these
Floor 5 (P): coffee; floor 3 (S): tea; R: milk
Q cannot have juice, so Q has water and T has juice
questions.trap: Giving Q the tea because it lives near the middle.
wrongReasons: The tea drinker lives on floor 3, which is S
The topmost floor (P) drinks coffee
Q is explicitly not the juice drinker

questions.text: Two positions of the same cube are shown. Which number is on the face opposite to 3?
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 260 125" role="img"><polygon points="70,20 115,40 70,60 25,40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><polygon points="25,40 70,60 70,110 25,90" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><polygon points="70,60 115,40 115,90 70,110" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><text x="66" y="45" font-size="15">1</text><text x="40" y="82" font-size="15">2</text><text x="86" y="82" font-size="15">3</text><polygon points="190,20 235,40 190,60 145,40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><polygon points="145,40 190,60 190,110 145,90" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><polygon points="190,60 235,40 235,90 190,110" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><text x="186" y="45" font-size="15">1</text><text x="160" y="82" font-size="15">4</text><text x="206" y="82" font-size="15">2</text></svg>
questions.explanation: Between the two views the cube is turned about the vertical axis with 1 on top. The face 3, now hidden, has become the left face, so the left face in the second view (4) is opposite 3.
steps: Spot what the question tests: Dice: a face never appears together with its opposite.
Option A (2) is out: 2 is adjacent to 3 in the first view.
Option B (1) is out: 1 is adjacent to 3.
Option C (5) is out: 5 is not visible in either view, so it is not the face turning into view.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing 2, which shares an edge with 3 in both views.
So the answer is option D: 4.
questions.trap: Choosing 2, which shares an edge with 3 in both views.
questions.revise: Dice: a face never appears together with its opposite
wrongReasons: 2 is adjacent to 3 in the first view
1 is adjacent to 3
5 is not visible in either view, so it is not the face turning into view

questions.text: If '+' means '×', '−' means '÷', '×' means '−' and '÷' means '+', then what is the value of 18 − 3 + 4 × 6 ÷ 2 ?
steps: Expression: 18 ÷ 3 × 4 − 6 + 2
questions.trap: Evaluating the symbols as printed instead of substituting first.
wrongReasons: Stopped after multiplying; ignored − 6 + 2
Swapped the last two signs incorrectly
Slipped in the final subtraction and addition
questions.shortcut: Rewrite the whole expression with the new signs before computing anything.

questions.text: If a ⊕ b = 2a + b² − ab, then what is the value of (3 ⊕ 4) ⊕ 2 ?
questions.trap: Slipping on the −ab term or the order of a and b in the second step.
wrongReasons: Mis-evaluated the first bracket
Arithmetic slip in the second step
Sign slip in the −ab term
questions.shortcut: Evaluate the bracket first, then substitute its value as 'a' in the second step.

questions.text:
Find the missing number.

Row 1: 3, 5, 34
Row 2: 4, 6, 52
Row 3: 5, 7, ?
questions.explanation: In each row the third number is the sum of the squares of the first two: 3² + 5² = 34 and 4² + 6² = 52. So 5² + 7² = 25 + 49 = 74.
questions.trap: Testing a × b patterns which do not fit the first row.
wrongReasons: Added a stray 2 to the sum of squares
Took 7² as 47
Used a × b + 35
questions.shortcut: 34 and 52 are both a sum of two squares; try that before anything more exotic.

questions.text:
Find the missing number.

Column 1: 2, 14, 5
Column 2: 3, 33, 8
Column 3: 4, ?, 7
questions.explanation: In each column the middle number equals (top × bottom) + top². Check: 2 × 5 + 4 = 14 and 3 × 8 + 9 = 33. For column 3: 4 × 7 + 16 = 44.
steps: Column 1: 2 × 5 + 2² = 14
Column 2: 3 × 8 + 3² = 33
questions.trap: Forgetting the squared top number and stopping at 28.
questions.revise: Column patterns with products and squares
wrongReasons: Used 4 × 7 + 14
Added 18 instead of 4²
questions.shortcut: The middle number equals top × (top + bottom): 2 × 7 = 14, 3 × 11 = 33, 4 × 11 = 44.

questions.text:
In the following question, the symbols have their usual meanings. Statements: P ≥ Q > R = S ≤ T < U

Conclusions:
I. Q > S
II. P > S
III. U > Q

Which of the conclusions definitely follow(s)?
options: All I, II and III follow
questions.explanation: Q > R = S gives Q > S (I). P ≥ Q > S gives P > S (II). U > T ≥ S gives only U > S; there is no link between T and Q, so U > Q (III) is not certain.
steps: Q > R and R = S, so Q > S: I follows
P ≥ Q and Q > S, so P > S: II follows
U > T and T ≥ S, so U > S only
T and Q are on different branches, so U > Q is not certain: III fails
questions.trap: Assuming a numeric ordering that the chain does not give.
wrongReasons: III cannot be derived: T and Q are not linked
III cannot be derived from the chain
II also follows through P ≥ Q > S
questions.shortcut: A conclusion holds only if the chain runs in one direction between the two terms.

questions.text: If 5 March 2024 was a Tuesday, what day of the week will 5 March 2027 be?
questions.explanation: From 5 March 2024 to 5 March 2027 there are three ordinary years, because the next leap day (29 February 2028) is after the date. 3 × 365 = 1095 days = 156 weeks + 3 days. Tuesday + 3 = Friday.
steps: Check for 29 February between the two dates: none (2025, 2026, 2027 are not leap years)
1095 days = 156 weeks + 3 odd days
Tuesday + 3 days = Friday
questions.trap: Counting the 2024 leap day, which falls before 5 March.
wrongReasons: Counted only 2 odd days
Counted 4 odd days by including the 2024 leap day, which is before 5 March
Counted only 1 odd day
questions.shortcut: Each normal year moves the weekday by 1; three years move it by 3.
